title: Ovid: Change as Story
subtitle: A Roman poem opens with transformation

proem.author: Ovid

proem.excerpt: My design leads me to speak of forms changed into new bodies.[1] Ye Gods, (for you it was who changed them,) favor my attempts,[2] and bring down the lengthened narrative from the very beginning of the world, {even} to my own times.[3]

daphne.excerpt: Her strength being {now} spent, she grows pale, and being quite faint, with the fatigue of so swift a flight, looking upon the waters of Peneus, she says, “Give me, my father, thy aid, if you rivers have divine power. Oh Earth, either yawn {to swallow me}, or by changing it, destroy that form, by which I have pleased too much, and which causes me to be injured.” Hardly had she ended her prayer, {when} a heavy torpor seizes her limbs; {and} her soft breasts are covered with a thin bark. Her hair grows into green leaves, her arms into branches; her feet, the moment before so swift, adhere by sluggish roots; a {leafy} canopy overspreads her features; her elegance alone[84] remains in her.

narrativeBlocks.title: Bodies changed into new forms
narrativeBlocks.body: Ovid opens the Metamorphoses with a promise: his poem is of shapes changed into new bodies, spun as one unbroken song from the world's creation down to his own day — nothing stable, everything becoming.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why change?
narrativeBlocks.body: For Ovid, transformation is the world's one constant: pursued nymphs become trees, grieving mothers become stone, beloved boys become flowers, emperors become stars. Every myth is a change of state.

narrativeBlocks.title: Apollo's first desire
narrativeBlocks.body: Fresh from killing the serpent Python, Apollo mocks Cupid's toy bow — and Cupid answers with two arrows: gold for Apollo, so he burns with desire for the nymph Daphne; lead for her, so she recoils from love entirely.

narrativeBlocks.title: The chase and the laurel
narrativeBlocks.body: Apollo hunts her through the woods, listing his glories as he runs — at the river's edge Daphne prays to her father the river-god to destroy her beauty. Bark closes over her legs, leaves crown her hair: she becomes the laurel tree.

narrativeBlocks.title: The laurel as memorial
narrativeBlocks.body: Apollo claims the tree as his own: laurel will crown his lyre, his poets, Rome's victors. Ovid's pattern is set — every transformation is both a loss and a monument.
